text:
Garry Kasparov, born Garik Kimovich Weinstein in Baku, Azerbaijan, Soviet Union, began his serious study of chess at age seven after solving a problem set by his parents. He trained under Mikhail Botvinnik and Vladimir Makogonov, winning the Soviet Junior Championship at age 13 and becoming a Grandmaster at 18. Rising rapidly through international competitions, Kasparov became the youngest world No. 1 in 1984 and the youngest world champion in 1985, defeating Anatoly Karpov in a closely contested match. He held the world title for over a decade, winning five world championship matches against Karpov and maintaining the top rating for 255 months.
In 1993, Kasparov broke with FIDE, forming the Professional Chess Association (PCA) to challenge FIDE's authority over the world championship. This led to a split in the title, with Kasparov as the PCA champion and FIDE champion Karpov remaining in the FIDE system until 2000. After losing the 2000 match to Vladimir Kramnik, Kasparov retired from regular competitive chess in 2005, citing a lack of personal goals and frustration over the failure to reunify the world championship.
Post-retirement, Kasparov remained active in chess, playing in exhibitions, simultaneous games, and rapid/blitz events. He coached Magnus Carlsen for a year, significantly influencing Carlsen's development. He also contributed to chess education, launched Kasparov Chess (a subscription-based online community), and participated in major tournaments like the Grand Chess Tour and 9LX.
Beyond chess, Kasparov became a prominent political figure, criticizing the Russian government under Vladimir Putin. He founded the United Civil Front, opposed Putin's policies, and was involved in anti-Putin campaigns. In 2013, he fled Russia due to fear of persecution and has since lived in exile, remaining a vocal critic of Putin's regime. He has also supported democratic movements in Armenia, advocated for human rights, and criticized authoritarianism in various international contexts.
Kasparov authored numerous books, including the acclaimed "My Great Predecessors" series, which explores the lives and careers of past world champions. He has also written on broader topics such as decision-making, artificial intelligence, and historical revisionism, promoting the idea that chess reflects real-world strategic thinking. His legacy includes a profound impact on modern chess theory, a dynamic playing style, and a sustained commitment to promoting democracy and human rights.
